introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2020. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain the concept of the Rank-Size Rule as postulated by G.K Zipf.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The Rank-Size Rule** is a statistical regularity in the size distribution of the cities of a country or region that was put forward by the American linguist **George Kingsley Zipf** (1949), building on observations by Auerbach and Jefferson, as a model of urban hierarchy.

**The rule.** If the cities of a country are ranked in descending order of population, the population of any city is inversely proportional to its rank:

$$P_n = \frac{P_1}{n}$$

where $P_n$ is the population of the city of rank $n$ and $P_1$ is the population of the largest city. So the second city has half the population of the largest, the third has one third, the fourth one quarter, and so on. **Illustration (hypothetical):** if the largest city has 1 000 000 people, the next ones have about 500 000, 333 000, 250 000 and 200 000. Plotted on **logarithmic graph paper** (rank on the horizontal axis and population on the vertical axis), a country that follows the rule gives a **straight line sloping down at about 45 degrees**.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

**Interpretation.**
- Conformity to the rule suggests a **mature, well-integrated urban system** with many cities of different sizes, resulting from a long history of urbanisation, a well-developed economy and good communications; it is approximately shown by larger and older urban systems such as the USA and Germany.
- Deviations are common. A **primate-city pattern** (one city much larger than twice the size of the second, such as Bangkok or Lima) occurs in smaller or less urbanised countries, or those with a strong colonial or centralised capital. A **binary or bi-polar pattern** exists where two cities are of similar size (for example Douala and Yaounde in Cameroon). A pattern with many middle-sized cities may occur in countries with federal systems or several regional centres.

**Limits of the rule:** it is a descriptive generalisation, not a law; it gives no explanation, depends on how a "city" is defined and where its boundaries are drawn, and takes no account of political, economic or physical factors, but it is useful for comparing countries and planning the urban hierarchy.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Examine **three** factors that influence *any one* of the following:

(i) the dispersion of rural settlements

(ii) the segregation of functions within a city.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Factors influencing the dispersion of rural settlements.** Rural settlements may be **dispersed** (isolated farms or scattered homesteads) or **nucleated** (villages). Dispersion is encouraged by the following.

1. **Water supply.** Where water is available almost everywhere (a high water table, many springs, streams or rain in sufficient amounts), people need not cluster around a few wet points and may settle scattered over the land. A scarce water supply (limited wet points) concentrates people into nucleated villages.
2. **Land, farming system and relief.** Fertile, well-distributed land and an economy based on individual farms, where each family wants its fields close to the house (ranching, mixed farming, perennial crops such as coffee in the highlands), lead to dispersion. In rugged relief, scattered patches of cultivable land can only support dispersed homesteads. Examples: the scattered compounds of the Bamileke and Bamenda highlands, the farms of the American Midwest, Scandinavia and many upland areas.
3. **Security and social factors, land tenure and government policy.** In peaceful areas without a threat of raids, defence by grouping is not needed and people settle on their own farmland. Individual land ownership, land enclosure and inheritance of separate plots favour scattered farms, while communal tenure, kinship ties and rural planning (for example villagisation policies in Tanzania or along roads in the forest zone) concentrate people. Better roads and transport also allow farmers to live far from each other.

---

**Alternative (the candidate chooses only one of (i) and (ii)):**

**(ii) Factors influencing the segregation of functions within a city.** Urban land is divided into **functional zones** (central business district, industry, residential areas of different quality, administration, open spaces) because different activities compete for space and have different needs.

1. **Land values, rent and competition (the bid-rent principle).** Land close to the city centre is the most accessible and the most expensive, so only activities that can earn high returns per unit of land (shops, banks, offices) can afford it, while industry, low-density housing and other users that need larger areas are pushed outwards where the land is cheaper. Examples: Akwa and Bonanjo, the business and administrative core of Douala, compared with the industrial areas of Bassa and Bonaberi.
2. **Accessibility and transport.** Accessibility to workers, customers and suppliers leads functions to locate along main roads and near rail stations, ports and airports. Firms that depend on the transport of goods locate by ports, railways and ring roads, and shops cluster at the most accessible central points.
3. **Linkages, agglomeration and incompatibility between land uses, plus planning policy.** Similar activities cluster to share services and customers (banks, government departments, markets), and **incompatible** uses are separated, for instance noisy or polluting industry away from housing. **Zoning** by town planners and the physical site (flood plains, steep slopes) also separate functions, as do the **social status** and income of the residents (high-class areas such as Bastos in Yaounde are separated from low-income areas).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Discuss the role played by green belts and satellite towns in controlling urban sprawl.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Urban sprawl** is the uncontrolled and unplanned outward spread of a city, often at a low density and in a scattered pattern, over the surrounding rural land, which results in the loss of farmland, long journeys to work, traffic jams and high costs of services.

**Green belts.** A green belt is a **ring of protected open land** (farmland, woodland, parks and recreation grounds) around a built-up area where new building is strictly controlled by planning law. Its roles are to:
- **limit the physical growth** of the city and prevent neighbouring towns from merging;
- **protect farmland, countryside and wildlife habitats**, and provide a reserve of open space for recreation, which acts as the "lungs" of the city;
- **encourage the redevelopment and re-use of derelict inner-city land** (brownfield sites) instead of building on rural land.
Examples: the London Green Belt (established in the 1930s and 1940s), and green belts around Seoul and Ottawa.

**Satellite towns.** These are planned, self-contained towns built **beyond the green belt** or at a distance from the city, with their own housing, jobs, shops and services, and joined to the main city by road or rail. Their roles are to **absorb the overspill population** and industries from the crowded central city, **reduce housing shortages and congestion**, provide employment locally to reduce commuting, and direct growth to planned centres. Examples: the new towns around London such as Harlow and Stevenage, and Tema near Accra (a planned port and industrial town, often cited as a satellite of Accra).

**Evaluation.** Green belts and satellite towns together channel growth away from the city edge. However, green belts can raise land and house prices inside the city and cause "leap-frog" development beyond the belt with longer commuting journeys; satellite towns may remain dependent on the main city for work and services, and they are expensive to plan and to build. In many developing countries, the weak application of planning law and rapid migration to cities have reduced the effectiveness of these measures.
